nameStory: Mexican tea gets its name from its traditional use as a medicinal tea in Mexico and Central America. Also called 'epazote' in Spanish, this aromatic herb has been brewed into teas for centuries to treat digestive ailments and intestinal worms - hence another common name, 'wormseed.'
description: Mexican tea is a strongly scented annual herb that grows 1-4 feet tall with an upright, branching stem. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves with toothed edges that release a pungent, gasoline-like smell when crushed. Tiny greenish flowers cluster along the stems in dense spikes, followed by small black seeds. This weedy plant often pops up in disturbed soils and waste areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves with irregular teeth along the edges. When crushed, they release an incredibly strong, distinctive smell that's been described as gasoline mixed with turpentine - once you smell it, you'll never forget it.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers without petals, densely packed into narrow spikes along the upper stems and leaf joints. The flower clusters feel slightly sticky to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, much-branched plant reaching 1-4 feet tall with a somewhat bushy appearance. The main stem is often reddish-tinged and feels smooth but sturdy.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces abundant tiny, shiny black seeds that fall easily from the plant when ripe. The seeds have a slight sheen and are about the size of poppy seeds.

habitat: Mexican tea thrives in disturbed soils like vacant lots, roadsides, gardens, and waste areas throughout New England's warmer regions. It prefers rich, nitrogen-rich soils and full sun, often appearing as a weedy volunteer in vegetable gardens and compost areas. Most commonly found in urban and suburban areas rather than wild natural habitats.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge in late spring with small, tender leaves that already carry the characteristic pungent smell when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full leafy growth and greenish flower spikes appearing in mid to late summer along the stems.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue flowering into early fall, producing abundant small black seeds before being killed by the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil for next year's growth.

funFact: Despite its off-putting gasoline-like smell, Mexican tea is actually an important culinary herb in Mexican cuisine, where it's added to bean dishes not just for flavor but because it genuinely reduces the gas-producing effects of beans!
confusionNotes: Mexican tea might be confused with other weedy amaranth family members, but its incredibly strong, petroleum-like smell when crushed is unmistakable - no other New England plant smells quite like this. Memory trick: 'Mexican tea smells like gasoline, but it's actually a cuisine!'
contextualKnowledge: This plant was formerly classified as Chenopodium ambrosioides and may still appear under that name in older field guides. Despite being called 'tea,' beginners should not experiment with brewing this plant, as it contains compounds that can be toxic in large quantities.
compareHints: Mexican tea differs from its relatives like clammy goosefoot and Jerusalem oak primarily by its much stronger, more pungent smell and its narrow, lance-shaped leaves. While other Dysphania species may have aromatic leaves, none have the intense gasoline-like odor of Mexican tea. Jerusalem oak has more deeply lobed, oak-like leaves, while clammy goosefoot has broader, more diamond-shaped leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like Mexican tea and Jerusalem oak, clammy goosefoot is much smaller and has the distinctive sticky texture.

Unlike its Dysphania relatives like Mexican tea (which has a strong, pungent odor when crushed) or clammy goosefoot (which feels sticky), winged pigweed is distinguished by its papery stem wings and lack of strong scent.
Jerusalem oak stands out from its Dysphania relatives by its deeply cut, almost fern-like leaves - Mexican tea and clammy goosefoot have much simpler, less divided leaves.
